Chapter 1
Introduction
“The intersection of education, technology, and innovation is a dynamic field where
challenges become opportunities and disciplines merge to redefine the future of
learning”
Education credentials, such as degrees, certificates and transcripts, have long been re-
garded as “prerequisites for employment” and “universal currency” in exchanging for
better job opportunities and social status in the labour market [1]. However, traditional
credentialing systems, including digital formats, face significant global challenges, such
as credential forgery and data breaches [2–5]. The proliferation of credentials issued
by diverse online education providers has exacerbated these credibility issues, resulting
in increasingly fragmented and difficult-to-verify learning records [4, 6–8]. This thesis
leverages blockchain technology and cryptographic techniques to address these press-
ing challenges by developing a blockchain-based educational credentialing system that
ensures both the trustworthiness of credentials and the privacy of users. An industry-
grounded study was conducted to enhance the system’s potential for adoption within the
education sector by incorporating usability considerations into the engineering process.
Besides, our proposed Decentralized Anonymous Credential (DAC) scheme not only
ensures essential security properties — such as unforgeability, anonymity, and unlinka-
bility — but also empowers users with greater authority over their credentials through
selective disclosure mechanism. Together, these contributions form the foundation of
a conceptual framework termed Decentralized Learning Autonomy (DLA). DLA aligns
with the Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) architecture, providing individuals with greater
1
2
control and ownership over their educational achievements. In this introductory chapter,
we outline the study’s motivations, research questions, scope, and development phases
in detail, setting the stage for the contributions presented in the subsequent chapters.
1.1 Motivations
This research is motivated by three categories of challenges, namely, educational creden-
tial challenges, blockchain adoption challenges, and credential security limitations.
1.1.1 Education Credential Challenges
Education is a significant investment for both governments and individuals. OECD
countries, for example, spend an average of 4.9% of their GDP on the education sector,
with individuals’ contributions accounts for about 30% of the total education investment
[9]. Despite this huge expenditure, individual learners still have to face a severe trend of
“credential inflation”. A 2018 survey highlights that 40% of employers have increased
job requirements related to educational credentials compared to five years ago, and 64%
report that the job market demands more credentials than ever before [10]. This rising
expectation intensifies the pressure on learners to accumulate more credentials (e.g.
967,734 credentials were issued in one year in the U.S based on a report of Credential
Engine in 2021)[6]. The following problems are becoming more serious under this big
background:
•Fragmented Learning Records : Educational credentials not only increased
in volume, but also evolved into various alternative forms [7]. Micro-credentials,
defined by the European Commission [11], are proofs of learning outcomes ac-
quired through short learning experiences, which often result in fragmented learn-
ing records. This fragmentation not only makes it difficult to track continuous
progress but also leads to the difficulty of credential proofs of the holder’s skills
[8]. The increasing volume and various types of credentials issued by different ed-
ucation providers from heterogeneous education systems exacerbate the credibility
problems in the educational credentialing ecosystem.
3
•Identity Theft & Credential Misuse : Credential forgery has become a global
issue, with numerous credential factories selling fake diplomas, degrees, and tran-
scripts [4]. A private university in India sold 36,000 fake degrees for $1,362 each,
causing graduates in Singapore, Malaysia, the US, and Canada to face pressure
from employers worldwide to verify their qualifications [2]. Additionally, 150 In-
dian students in Canada faced deportation after being victims of an immigration
scam that provided them with forged college admission letters [3]. On the other
hand, honest students holding authentic certificates are at risk of credential misuse
and theft, as demonstrated by LinkedIn’s 2021 breach, which resulted in 700 mil-
lion users’ profiles being sold on the Dark Web [5]. Such incidents expose authentic
credential holders to potential exploitation, further complicating the verification
of educational qualifications in a digital world.
•Centralized Credentials Governance : Current credentialing systems rely heav-
ily on centralized third-party platforms. For instance, 55 universities in Australia
and New Zealand utilize a centralized credentialing platform – MyeQuals – to is-
sue verifiable credentials, storing data centrally in one location. This centralized
model introduces a single point of failure, posing significant risks to the privacy
and security of over 1.6 million learners and 4.8 million documents [12].
•Deteriorating Trust and Value : Growing skepticism toward traditional cre-
dentialing systems has led major corporations, such as Google and Amazon, to
develop their own internal credentialing programs. These initiatives highlight de-
clining confidence in the existing systems and their perceived inadequacy in meet-
ing industry needs [13].
These complex and multi-dimensional problems call for innovative solutions that restore
trust, ensure data integrity, and enable decentralized control over credential records.
Blockchain technology has been proposed as a promising response, offering features such
as data availability, tamper-resistance, and verifiability that directly align with the needs
of modern credentialing systems [14–16]. Research on blockchain in education began to
emerge around 2016 and reached its peak in 2019 [17]. However, like its application in
other sectors such as healthcare, supply chain, and smart cities, blockchain adoption in
education has faced bottlenecks in implementation and challenges to achieve a large-scale
sustainable impact since 2019 [18]. Existing studies primarily focus on literature reviews
4
[7, 17, 19] or technical prototypes [20–25], often lacking engagement with the broader
educational context. To build on this foundation, our research begins by investigating
the following questions:
•RQ1: Can blockchain technology provide a feasible solution to the challenges in
educational credentialing?
•RQ2: What are the existing blockchain-based solutions in education, and how can
we evaluate their effectiveness?
1.1.2 Blockchain Opportunities & Challenges
Blockchain technology, first introduced through Bitcoin in response to the 2008 financial
crisis, has demonstrated significant potential to solve trust issues across various indus-
tries, including supply chain management, healthcare, and education [26]. Deloitte’s
2021 Global Blockchain Survey underscores this trend, where 78% of 1,280 surveyed
senior executives across ten global locations perceive a compelling business value for
integrating blockchain technology into their organizations or projects [27]. In the field
of education, blockchain applications have also gained substantial attention and can be
classified into several areas: degree verification , educational record management, pro-
fessional ability evaluation for students, institutional management systems, and online
learning environments [28–33]. Each of these applications demonstrates the promising
potential of blockchain to address specific challenges within educational ecosystems.
Despite these industrial recognitions, the real-world adoption of blockchain technology
has fallen considerably short of expectations. Lacity et al [34] report that the majority of
blockchain applications existed as prototypes, merely 10% of their surveyed organizations
had implemented one single blockchain application, and none of these deployments had
been scaled up. Given this context, researchers have begun investigating the reasons
behind this low adoption phenomenon. These studies generally fall into three broad
categories, including:
•Technical Challenges : Scalability, performance, and interoperability are widely
recognized as significant obstacles. While these issues dominate current research,
practical and widely applicable solutions remain elusive [34, 35].
5
•Human Factors : Human challenges, such as user acceptability and the transi-
tion to new business models, along with societal factors like laws and regulatory
support, have been identified as crucial factors, albeit less studied [35–37]. Fur-
thermore, the lack of user-centered evaluations and limited engagement between
blockchain developers and industry stakeholders have contributed to a disconnect
between technical solutions and real-world needs [31].
•Engineering Methods : From an engineering perspective, inadequate project
management and unsystematic development have been identified as the major fac-
tor contributing to the failure of blockchain projects [38, 39]. To address these
issues, various blockchain software engineering frameworks have been proposed
[39, 40]. However, most of the existing studies propose just conceptual frame-
works, integrating blockchain into established software engineering fragments, and
exploring their interrelations. Despite some of these studies are constructed based
on Grounded Theory, utilizing data sourced from literature or interviews with
blockchain developers, they lack insights drawn from first-hand experiences of de-
veloping a practical blockchain application. Besides, none of these frameworks has
been thoroughly tested in real-world scenarios or achieved universal agreement.
These challenges highlight the need for an interdisciplinary approach that combines
technical innovation with social and usability considerations. Such an approach is critical
to lowering the barriers to blockchain adoption, particularly in the education sector,
where user-centered design and practical implementation must align with the sector’s
unique requirements. To guide this effort, the following research questions are proposed:
•RQ3: What socio-technical factors influence blockchain adoption in education?
•RQ4: How can tailored engineering methodologies address these factors to create
usable and scalable blockchain-based solutions?
1.1.3 SSI Solution Limitations
To solve the credential issues, Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI) is positioned as a promising
solution [41–43], under the shift towards the Web 3.0 paradigm where “user sovereignty”
gains increased attention [44]. An SSI system that can provide “user sovereignty” should
6
satisfy the following requirements [41–43, 45, 46]: 1) users’ full control over their identi-
ties, 2) minimized data disclosure for a constrained use, 3) decentralized data storage, 4)
selective sharing to chosen entities and 5) the creation of consistent and portable identi-
ties. Education credentials enforced by SSI can be nested with new attributes, such as
security, portability and self-autonomy [47]. A specific application case is the “Diploma
Use case” of the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure (EBSI), which is built on
the European Self-Sovereign Identity Framework [47]. In this case, cryptographic proofs
of digital diplomas will be stored on the blockchain and issued to learners’ wallets to
allow users full control of their identities and education data.
However, existing SSI systems face significant challenges in fully realizing these goals:
•Partial Decentralization : Industry initiatives like uPort, Sovrin, and ShoCard
have implemented SSI ideas in real-world scenarios, but their solutions have only
achieved partial decentralization in handling identity data [46, 48]. For instance,
uPort stores registration data in three types of smart contracts [49], where the data
security solely relies on the underlying code; Sovrin relies on blockchain clients for
the backup of registry data [50]; and ShoCard employs centralized servers [48, 51].
These applications focus predominantly on the application layer, often neglecting
authentication and authorization processes.
•Challenges in Fulfilling All Security Properties : Academic research has
made notable progress in achieving critical security properties. These include 1)
Unforgeability , which ensures that only genuine credentials issued by the stated
authority can pass verification protocols [52]; 2) Anonymity , which protects users’
identities by ensuring that interactions using pseudonyms cannot reveal real iden-
tities [53–56]; 3) Unlinkability : Prevents linking a user’s activities across multiple
transactions, preserving privacy [57, 58]; and 3) Revocation that enables revo-
cation of credentials in specific cases or reveals user identities under predefined
conditions [58–61]. However, achieving these properties simultaneously in a single
system remains a significant challenge [55, 58].
•Practice Limitations : Existing systems often fail to support critical functionali-
ties required in real-world applications, including: Selective Disclosure , the ability
to reveal only specific credentials or attributes while maintaining overall privacy,
7
which remains largely underdeveloped [62]; and Unbounded Attributes , as many
systems fix the attributes during the setup phase, limiting their flexibility and
scalability for users who may need to manage evolving or diverse credentials over
time [63].
These challenges highlight the need for an innovative credential scheme that seamlessly
integrates all the desired security properties with real-world usability and flexibility.
This leads to the following research questions:
•RQ5: How can we design a secure and privacy-preserving credential scheme that
supports selective disclosure, unbounded attributes, and decentralized storage, while
simultaneously achieving essential security properties such as unforgeability, anonymity,
unlinkability, and revocation?
•RQ6: How can such a credentialing scheme be embedded into a blockchain system
to create a decentralized identity management platform for broader applications,
including education?
1.2 Research Scope and Thesis Structure
In response to the above-mentioned challenges, this thesis introduces the concept of De-
centralized Learning Autonomy (DLA), an educational paradigm that empowers learn-
ers with control over their educational credentials in a secure, verifiable, and privacy-
preserving manner. This concept integrates advancements in blockchain technology,
Self-Sovereign Identity (SSI), and credential verification, offering a vision for a learner-
centered, trustworthy, and verifiable credentialing ecosystem. DLA is not presented as
a rigid framework; instead, it serves as an integrative concept that emerges from the
contributions of each research study included in this work.
8
Definition
Decentralized Learning Autonomy (DLA) refers to an educational paradigm
that empowers learners with full control over their educational credentials, whether
obtained from traditional institutions, online platforms, or fragmented learning expe-
riences. Learners can aggregate diverse learning records, including micro-credentials,
to generate context-specific, verifiable proofs of their skills and achievements.
Leveraging blockchain technology, DLA ensures these credentials satisfy essential se-
curity properties, including unforgeability, anonymity, unlinkability, selective disclo-
sure, and revocation. This guarantees both learner privacy and credential verifiability
while fostering trust and accountability in the credentialing process.
Figure 1.1 illustrates the positioning of DLA at the intersection of Blockchain Applica-
tion, SSI, and Education Credentials. The framework leverages blockchain technology
as the foundational “root of trust” and aligns with the layered architecture of SSI to
ensure privacy, security, and autonomy in education credential management.

2.1 Distributed Ledger Technology
The Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT), specifically blockchain in our study, forms
the foundational layer in the SSI structure, offering a “root of trust” for decentral-
ized credentialing systems. Blockchain’s key properties – such as decentralization, im-
mutability, transparency, and tamper resistance – make it particularly suitable for ap-
plications where trust and data integrity are essential, such as educational credentialing
[44]. Blockchain operates as a distributed ledger in which a series of blocks store digital
data. Each block contains a set of validated transactions, a timestamp, and a crypto-
graphic hash of the preceding block, thus forming an unbroken, tamper-resistant chain
[14]. This structure ensures that once data is added to the blockchain, it becomes vir-
tually immutable, enhancing trustworthiness in credential management by preventing
unauthorized data modification or deletion.
2.1.1 Adopted Blockchains
Blockchain technology has seen the emergence of hundreds of platforms, each tailored
for specific use cases and with varying levels of decentralization, scalability, and secu-
rity. In this research, we adopt both permissionless (e.g. Algorand and Ethereum)
and permissioned (e.g. Hyperledger Fabric) blockchain platforms to implement different
prototypes. The rationale for adopting these platforms is detailed below:
•Ethereum addresses the limitations of Bitcoin’s scripting language by introducing
a blockchain with a built-in, Turing-complete programming language [15]. This
flexibility allows Ethereum to support a wide range of applications, including both
financial and non-financial use cases, such as identity and reputation systems and
decentralized file storage. Ethereum’s extensive developer ecosystem and smart
contract capabilities make it a strong candidate for implementing decentralized
credentialing systems.
•Algorand excels as a competitive solution to the blockchain trilemma, addressing
scalability, security, and decentralization challenges effectively [67, 68]. Its consis-
tently low transaction costs and scalable architecture align more closely with our
goal of creating a universally accessible and affordable platform. It also provides a
13
better development environment, offering user-friendly features like Atomic Trans-
fers and Algorand Standard Assets (ASAs), further contributing to an enhanced
usability experience.
•Hyperledger Fabric: Hyperledger Fabric is a permissioned blockchain platform
specifically designed for enterprise applications. Its modular architecture and fine-
grained access control make it well-suited for scenarios requiring privacy and scal-
ability. Fabric supports smart contracts (termed “chaincode”) written in widely
used programming languages like Go, Java, and Node.js provides flexibility and
ease of integration into existing enterprise systems.[69]
2.1.2 Consensus Mechanism
In blockchain systems, a consensus mechanism is crucial to ensure that all nodes agree on
the state of the ledger, particularly when transactions are being continuously appended.
A consensus mechanism must satisfy three essential properties: 1) consistency ensures
all nodes have a unified view of the transaction log; 2) liveness guarantees the inclu-
sion of new, valid transactions; and 3) serializability enforces a consistent ordering of
transactions, allowing the network to function as a coherent distributed ledger [70].
Prominent consensus mechanisms for blockchains include but not limited to proof-of-
work (PoW), proof-of-stake (PoS), and Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT). The following
reviews the specific consensus protocols used by the selected platforms:
•Ethereum originally employed the PoW consensus mechanism, using the Ethash
algorithm, which is designed to be ASIC-resistant to promote decentralization [71].
Ethash relies on a memory-intensive dataset to discourage the use of specialized
hardware, ensuring broad accessibility. Currently, Ethereum is transitioning to
PoS through, “the merge”, a significant upgrade aimed at improving energy ef-
ficiency and scalability [72]. PoS selects validators to propose and attest to new
blocks based on the amount of cryptocurrency they have staked, reducing compu-
tational waste.
•Algorand employs a Pure Proof-of-Stake (PPoS) mechanism, which combines
randomness and cryptographic sortition to select validators. This ensures scala-
bility, security, and energy efficiency while maintaining decentralization. [67, 68]
14
•Hyperledger Fabric utilizes a unique Crash Fault-Tolerant (CFT) or Byzantine
Fault-Tolerant (BFT) consensus mechanism, tailored for permissioned environ-
ments [69]. Unlike public blockchains, Fabric’s consensus process involves only
pre-authorized nodes, providing enhanced transaction throughput and privacy.
2.1.3 Smart Contract
Smart contracts are self-executing programs that encode complex, programmable logic
on a blockchain, enabling automated and trustless execution of predefined conditions.
Smart contracts are a fundamental component of blockchain technology, facilitating a
wide range of decentralized applications ( DApps ).
Ethereum pioneered the use of smart contracts in blockchain ecosystems, offering a
Turing-complete environment for decentralized computation [15, 71]. Ethereum’s smart
contracts are written in Solidity, a high-level programming language designed specifically
for the Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM). The EVM executes smart contracts in a
sandboxed, decentralized manner, ensuring that code execution is deterministic and
tamper-resistant. Solidity supports advanced features such as inheritance, libraries, and
interfaces, making it suitable for developing decentralized finance (DeFi) applications,
token standards (e.g., ERC-20, ERC-721), and complex decentralized ecosystems .
Algorand categorizes smart contracts into two main types: stateful contracts and state-
less contracts (also known as smart signatures). Stateful contracts maintain on-chain
state, whereas stateless contracts primarily approve or reject transactions. Smart con-
tracts on Algorand are written in Transaction Execution Approval Language (TEAL),
an assembly-like language processed by the Algorand Virtual Machine (AVM). TEAL
is Turing-complete, supporting looping and subroutines, which enables advanced pro-
grammability. Additionally, smart contracts can be written in PyTeal, a Python library
that compiles to TEAL for enhanced developer convenience. [73].
In contrast to permissionless blockchains like Ethereum and Algorand, Hyperledger Fab-
ric[69] is a permissioned blockchain framework tailored for enterprise use. Fabric uses
chaincode, which are smart contracts written in Go, Java, or Node.js, to define the busi-
ness logic for transactions. Chaincode is executed by endorsing peers, and then verified
by other nodes before being appended to the ledger. Such a distributed feature of the
15
blockchain, integrating with smart contracts [74], allows users to deploy applications on
the blockchain without the involvement of any trusted authority. This design enhances
performance, scalability, and privacy, making Hyperledger Fabric particularly suitable
for enterprise-level applications
2.2 Decentralized Identifiers
Decentralized Identifiers (DIDs), as defined by W3C standards [75], are defined as glob-
ally unique, persistent identifiers, which are generated cryptographically. Unlike tra-
ditional identifiers that rely on a centralized registration authority, DIDs are designed
to function in decentralized systems, making them a cornerstone of self-sovereign iden-
tity frameworks.[75]. DIDs form a critical component of Verifiable Credentials (VC),
by providing a secure and verifiable means of identifying the subject and issuer of a
credential. [75, 76]. Cryptographic material associated with DIDs, specifically the pub-
lic keys listed in the DID document, is essential for verifying the digital signatures of
Verifiable Credentials. Issuers use their private keys to sign credentials, while verifiers
rely on the corresponding public keys from the DID document to authenticate the sig-
natures. Furthermore, DIDs support enhanced privacy through pairwise DIDs – unique
identifiers created for each relationship – ensuring that interactions between credential
holders, issuers, and verifiers are isolated and cannot be correlated.
An illustrative use case of DIDs can be found in educational credentials. For example,
Alice, a graduate of the University of Oxford, receives a Verifiable Credential for her
degree that is linked to her DID [77]. Alice’s DID document, representing her identity,

2.3 Credential Layer
The Credential Layer addresses how verified attributes, or credentials, are managed,
stored, and shared in decentralized systems. This layer is critical for ensuring the in-
tegrity, authenticity, and privacy of educational credentials in the DLA framework.
Figure 2.2: Triangle of Trust
Effective credentialing requires addressing the Triangle of Trust, encompassing three pil-
lars (see Fig. 2.2 (a)), namely: identity , defining ’who’s who’; ownership , outlining ’who
owns what’; and verification , certifying ’what’s true’[33] . The credentialing workflow
embodies these principles, establishing a Triangle of Trust structure [66]. Within this
framework (refer to Fig 2.2 (b)), there are three key actors who work around onetrust
dependency data component:
•Credentials are authenticated documents or statements that validate an indi-
vidual’s qualifications or affiliations [54]. They can be either single-use, like a
prescription, or multiple-use, and might have expiration dates. In the realm of
education, for instance, credentials such as degrees, certificates, and transcripts
serve as pivotal evidence for recruiters assessing an applicant’s aptitude [29].
•Holder : Entities that utilize credentials to certify their identity or credentials to
Verifiers.
•Issuer : Entities that generate and attest claims about subjects, translating these
assertions into credentials which are subsequently issued to Holders.
•Verifier : Those responsible for validating the cryptographic integrity of creden-
tials, ensuring that they originate from legitimate Issuers and are presented by
authentic Holders.
18
2.3.1 Anonymous Credentials
Anonymous credentials have been proven to be a pivotal solution to balance security and
privacy protection in user-centric identity management since 1985 [53, 56, 78]. Chaum
[53] pioneered this domain by introducing the concept of “digital pseudonyms” where
pseudonyms are created and managed to ensure user privacy during communications.
Then, Lysyanskaya et al. [54] provide a formal definition of pseudonym systems that
minimize the involvement of a trusted center and achieve unlinkability between differ-
ent pseudonyms. The field further evolved with Camenisch and Lysyanskaya’s work
[55], introducing non-transferability and optional anonymity revocation for particular
transactions. Subsequent studies focus on enhancing credential privacy and efficiency
through various signature schemes [78]. Works by Camenisch et al. [79] and Kaaniche
et al. [80] adopt attribute-based signatures for improved access control. Belenkiy et al.
[78] create non-interactive P-signatures that streamline the certificate acquisition pro-
cess. However, despite these advancements in anonymity, unlinkability, and efficiency,
challenges such as a lack of transparency and centralized control remain unsolved.
2.3.2 Decentralized Anonymous Credentials (DAC)
To reduce the trust of centralized authorities in the credential issuing, decentralized
anonymous credential (DAC) based on the blockchain was proposed by Garman et al
[60], where users construct and manage their credentials in a fully anonymous manner.
However, this full anonymity could compromise the accountability of the credentials, as it
depends on user-provided metadata and difficulty in tracking users’ historical behaviours.
The Coconut scheme [63] enhanced the credential accountability by requiring only a
subset of authorities to issue partial credentials, thereby enabling users to generate
a consolidated credential. Yet, Coconut faces limitations due to its fixed number of
attributes and does not support credential revocation.
To enhance the application of DAC, recent studies start to explore the design of De-
centralized Identity Management Systems (DIMS). Damgard et al. [57] introduced re-
vocability protocols, where a collaboration between issuers and revokers can unveil user
identity data. However, this approach still relies on issuers for data storage. CanDID [58]
introduces a Deduplication protocol to counter Sybil attacks, but a challenge arises with
19
the continuously expanding size of the locally stored IDTable required for this dedupli-
cation process. The most recent work [66] describes a post-quantum verifiable credential
scheme based on lattices, but it lacks solution of selective disclosure. Li et al.[62] employ
attribute-based credentials, similar to our idea, but do not address batched verification.
Current DAC studies face several challenges that we seek to improve in this work (as
detailed in Chapter 5).
2.4 Decentralized Application
Decentralised applications (DApps) have various architectural patterns, each with pros
and cons regarding decentralisation, efficiency, and scalability [81]. In Peer-to-Peer
(P2P) Architecture , every node on the network functions as both a client and a server.
This model is fundamental to many DApps, particularly those focused on file sharing
(e.g. IPFS [82]) or decentralised messaging apps (e.g. Status [83]). The Client-Server
with Decentralised Backend architecture divides DApp components between client-side
interfaces and a decentralised backend. The backend manages core logic and data storage
on the blockchain, ensuring transparency and immutability for critical operations. This
pattern is frequently used in decentralised storage services like Filecoin [84]. The Off-
Chain with On-Chain Settlement pattern processes computations off-chain for speed
and cost-effectiveness while leveraging blockchain for final settlements, exemplified by
payment channels like the Lightning Network [85] and Raiden Network [86]. Hybrid
Decentralised Architectures combine blockchain for critical data and traditional servers
for performance,(e.g. Steem [87]). Finally, Fully Decentralised (On-Chain) Architecture
places all components, including UI and logic, on-chain for maximum transparency and
security, often seen in DeFi platforms (e.g., Uniswap [88]) and voting systems (e.g.,
Horizon State [89]).

A typical hybrid DApp architecture can be exemplified using an Ethereum-based DApp,
as illustrated in Figure 2.3. This architecture comprises two primary subsystems: the
On-chain Subsystem and the Off-chain Subsystem. The on-chain subsystem includes
smart contracts, which are self-executing programs that manage business logic, han-
dle state transitions, and execute immutable transactions, running within the Ethereum
Virtual Machine (EVM). The EVM, operating on every blockchain node, ensures consis-
tent execution and isolates smart contracts to maintain blockchain integrity. Distributed
nodes validate transactions, propagate state changes, and maintain the decentralized
ledger. The off-chain subsystem enhances scalability and user interaction through a
user interface (UI) that serves as the primary access point for users. A traditional
server complements the blockchain by managing business logic execution, storing sensi-
tive or large-scale data, and facilitating blockchain communication, such as transaction
submissions and status updates. REST APIs connect the UI, server, blockchain, and
decentralized storage systems like the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS), which stores
large off-chain data and links it to the blockchain through content identifiers (hashes).
21
In a typical DApp architecture, users can interact with the blockchain through two
primary methods. The first method, User – Wallet – Blockchain , exemplifies direct
interaction where users initiate actions like sending cryptocurrency or executing smart
contracts via a wallet, such as Metamask for Ethereum or Pera Wallet for Algorand.
The wallet manages the user’s private keys, cryptographically signs transactions, and
directly communicates with the blockchain, ensuring a high degree of decentralization
and security. The second method, User – User Interface – Traditional Server – API –
Blockchain , is common in hybrid DApp architectures and integrates centralized compo-
nents for improved user experience. Here, the user interacts with a visual and interactive
interface hosted on a traditional server, which communicates with the blockchain via
APIs. While this method offers a smoother and more user-friendly experience, it intro-
duces a degree of centralization as the server acts as an intermediary. Both methods
ensure secure blockchain interaction, but the choice depends on the DApp’s design goals
and user needs.
2.5 Chapter Summary
This chapter introduce the preliminary concepts and review relevant studies that set
up the foundation to understand this research. In the next chapter, we will review the
education credentialing landscape, and theoretically analyse blockchain feasibility, most
importantly, we proposed a comparison framework to assess the comtempary blockchain-
based education systems.
Chapter 3
The Landscape of
Blockchain-based Solutions for
Education Credentials
“Research is formalized curiosity. It is poking and prying with a purpose.”
— Zora Neale Hurston
This chapter examines the landscape of blockchain-based credentialing within the con-
text of the Australian tertiary education system. It introduces an abstract credentialing
workflow, maps the roles of key stakeholders and outlines five desired attributes of an
ideal credentialing infrastructure. Additionally, this chapter presents a layered frame-
work for evaluating seven blockchain-based education projects, offering insights into
the barriers to their broader adoption. Finally, it proposes considerations to guide our
next-stage development of blockchain-based solutions for educational credentialing.
3.1 Introduction
Blockchain technology has been introduced and adopted as a new solution to addressing
education credentialing problems with attributes to ensure data availability, verifiability,
and trustworthiness. The relevant studies started in 2016, boosted in 2018 and peaked in
2019 [17]. However, similar to many other industries, such as supply chain, healthcare
22
23
and smart cities, blockchain adoption in education has also encountered bottlenecks
since 2019 with limited implementation and scaling[18]. Current studies can broadly be
categorized into two groups based on research questions and methodologies. One group
encompasses systematic literature reviews [7, 17, 19], exploring the potentialities of
blockchain and how relevant studies have developed over the years. Another group falls
into technical prototype designs [20–25] that explores how to develop a blockchain-based
application to solve particular educational problems; some of them tend to jump straight
into the prototype development stage without careful examination of the education
landscape. However, both types of studies offer limited insights into factors that may
hinder the adoption of blockchain technology in education.
Therefore, our research, built on top of previous studies, aims to fill this gap by exploring
obstacles that may hinder blockchain adoption as a reflection and to provide implications
as a navigation tool for future development. We make the following contributions in this
chapter:
•We depict a succinct credentialing workflow with the purpose of providing a de-
scription of the education credentialing landscape.
•We identify the prevailing problems that major stakeholders face, propose five
desired attributes of ideal credentials infrastructure and highlight corresponding
blockchains features that can support these desired attributes.
•We propose a four-layer framework for comparing existing blockchain-based stud-
ies, and discuss the potential reasons that may hinder the large-scale adoption
from interdisciplinary perspectives.
The rest of the chapter is structured as follows: Section 3.2 describes the education
credentialing landscape and emerging problems. Section 3.3 presents the key features
of blockchain technology that can benefit the credentialing system. In Section 3.4, we
specify the four-layer comparison framework in details and explore the implications for
future development.
24
3.2 The Typical Process of Education Credentialing
This section sets the stage for exploring how blockchain can address the challenges in-
herent in traditional credentialing practices. It begins with a high-level description of
the education credentialing process, identifies existing problems in the industry, and
proposes desired characteristics of ideal credentials infrastructure. Each higher educa-
tion system shares many commonalities, but they are also different due to historical
and legislative reasons. In the case of this study, we choose Australian Qualification
Framework (AQF) as a foundation for this study because it is a core element of the
regulatory architecture that underpins Australia’s quality education and aligns with in-
ternational frameworks [90]. Notably, the AQF supports the principles outlined in the
Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications concerning Higher Education,
adopted by UNESCO in 2019 [91]. This convention establishes universal principles for
the fair, transparent, and non-discriminatory recognition of higher education qualifica-
tions, thereby facilitating global academic mobility and cooperation.
3.2.1 Credentialing Workflow
Educational credentials refer to various types of evidence of learning achievements a
student may receive during a credentialing process, such as academic transcripts, place-
ments certificates, qualifications and degrees [47]. In general, the higher the entry re-
quirement and graduate threshold, the greater the value of a credential is [1]. The
contemporary education credentialing procedures can be summarized into four steps as
an illustration to clarify the complex landscape (see Figure 3.1):
1. Credentialing Programs: A student applies for a credential-targeted education pro-
gram provided by an accredited education provider, such as a Registered Training
Organisation (RTO) or a Higher Education Institution (HEI) in either traditional
or online form[90]. The student is required to provide evidence of previous study
and any relevant work experience in order to meet the education provider’s en-
trance criteria. After successfully passing the entrance assessment, the student
may receive an offer to enrol and start the education program.
25
2. Learning Credits or Micro-credentials: The student conducts learning activities
and passes corresponding assessment in order to gain either traditional learn-
ing credits or digital micro-credentials awarded by education providers. Micro-
credentials, often referred to as ’digital badges’ or ’nano-degrees,’ are emerging
terms in recent years, work similarly to learning credits that represent smaller
modules of learning and can accumulate into a larger credential (e.g. a degree)
[1]. The alternative names of micro-credentials include ’nano-degree,’ ’learning
badges,’ or ’endorsements’[23].
3. Education Credentials: After the student collects enough learning credits or micro-
credentials from required subjects and meets graduation criteria, they will be is-
sued education credentials by the education provider presented in forms of tran-
scripts, completion certificates, and qualifications to represent the student’s learn-
ing achievements;
4. Verifiable Credentials: After graduation, when the student applying a job or a
higher degree, they may be asked by recruiters (e.g. employers) to present certified
education credentials. A majority of Australian universities suggest their graduates
to use the My eQuals platform for getting a verifiable credential in forms of either
a secure link or a cryptographically signed PDF document [12].
Figure 3.1: Credentialing workflow and involved stakeholders
26
This is an ideal depiction of credentialing workflow, where credentials link every stake-
holder interacting with each other smoothly, mainly for a general understanding of the
tertiary education landscape. However, as discussed in Chapter 1, the growing complex-
ity of the education credentialing landscape is exacerbated by the increasing volume of
credentials issued by diverse education providers.
3.2.2 Desired Attributes of Education Credentials
Based on the analysis of the education credentialing landscape and the challenges iden-
tified, including difficulties in credential recognition [21], issues of forged and tampered
credentials [92], increased costs of hiring and verification [22, 93], and risks of identity
theft [12], we propose the following desired attributes for an ideal education credentialing
infrastructure:
•Learner control: The learners themselves should control and manage credentials,
not centralized third parties, to prevent data manipulation or misuse.
•Verifiable: The authenticity of credentials can be efficiently verified in easy ways.
The verification validity should not rely on human beings’ power.
•Tamper-free: Credentials should not be easily modified by any fraudulent be-
haviour. If any modification happens, it should be easily identified and tracked.
•Portability: Credentials should have the ability to overcome credentialing barri-
ers and can be carried along with learners to present flexibly between different
educational platforms and workplaces.
•Employability-driven: Credentials can provide industry-required knowledge and
skills for learners to keep competitiveness in the employment market.
3.3 Blockchain Empowers Credentialing
Blockchain technology, as a decentralized alternative, seems to support all the desired
characteristics listed above. It can empower education credentials lifecycle through mul-
tiple pathways. This section highlights the key features necessary for the education
27
credentialing scenario. Firstly, we describe the general attributes of blockchain that nu-
merous studies have mentioned, such as decentralization and immutability[7, 17, 19, 23–
25]. Then, we heighten two supplementary properties, self-sovereign and tokenization.
Despite not being considered in every study, these two properties have a great possibil-
ity of driving blockchain applications (known as DApps) to the next level[94]. Other
attributes, such as types of blockchain, smart contract and data storage, are discussed
as comparison points between selected prototypes in Section IV.
3.3.1 Decentralization
The distributed nature of blockchain data storage allows every node (ledger) of the sys-
tem has a verified backup of data [95]. This feature brings a higher level of data security
for students’ learning records since individuals can access their learning credentials from
any single node of the system [47]. Even if the student moves to another country’s
education system or loses original contact with the issuing institution, they can still
retrieve or recover learning credentials anywhere in the world. A decentralized peer-
to-peer network can also prevent fraudulent behaviours since it is impossible to change
their educational data on every archive in the network, which facilitates the verification
process and reduces employers’ recruitment screening costs.
3.3.2 Immutability
The second important feature of blockchain is immutability, which means that once a
learning credential has been recorded on the chain, it is impossible to be modified by
any party. Immutability can be achieved through the following mechanisms embedded
in blockchains: timestamp, hash function, consensus, and peer-to-peer network [23]. For
example, learning credentials can be sealed with a timestamp – a unique fingerprint in
chronological order, to track when the learner has achieved a credential. The hash func-
tion can convert credential documents (without limitations on size and length) into a
small-sized output, named ”digest” [96]. Even small changes on the original documents
will lead to dramatic changes on the output[96]. Therefore, fraudulent behaviours can
be easily detected. Besides, any modification on the chain has to face rigorous ap-
proval from the network participants in order to achieve global consensus. Thanks to
28
these attributes, blockchain technology can provide provenance for credentials, improve
verification efficiency, and help to rebuild trust between different stakeholders.
3.3.3 Self-sovereignty
Blockchain provides the solution to challenges, such as discontinuity of learning and iden-
tity theft mentioned above, through facilitating a new identity management paradigm –
self-sovereign identity (SSI) [97]. SSI means that individuals have complete control over
their data, and people can decide how their data is being used and disclosed without third
parties’ interventions[97]. Education credentials enforced by SSI can be nested with new
attributes, such as security, portability and self-autonomy. Moreover, the credentialing
system can inherit the properties of blockchain to provide not only privacy-secured shar-
ing but also across different geographical and political barriers [47]. A specific applica-
tion case is the ”Diploma Use case” of the European Blockchain Services Infrastructure
(EBSI), which is built on the European Self-Sovereign Identity Framework [47]. In this
case, cryptographic proofs of digital diplomas will be stored on the blockchain and issued
to learners’ wallets to allow users full control of their identities and education data.
3.3.4 Tokenization
Though merely discussed in related education studies, tokenization has been successfully
adopted in some real-life cases (e.g. Student Coin [98]) and opens a wide range of op-
portunities for future applications. By definition, the process of customizing digital data
or assets into a new cryptographic form using blockchain technologies, named tokens,
can be called ”tokenization” [94]. This process has been believed to improve business
processes efficiently and can vastly expand the DApps to a broader scope[94]. Based on
functionality, tokens can be classified into fungible tokens for exchangeable assets and
non-fungible tokens (NFTs) for indivisible assets. NFTs can prove ownership, protect
intellectual property, and, most importantly, can prevent counterfeiting and fraud prob-
lems in practice [94]. These distinguishable attributes shed light on solving the existing
credentialing problems. For instance, some pilots have used tokens to represent edu-
cation awards (e.g.E2C-Chain)[22], learning credits (e.g. EduCTX )[20], and education
reputation (e.g. Kudos)[99].
29
3.4 Blockchain Solutions Comparison Framework
Multiple academic and industry projects are ongoing or in their initial phases. In [100],
Authors used the snowballing approach in software engineering, built on a “start set”
[100] of recent systematic literature review studies [7, 17, 19], to select representative
studies. When filtering representative studies, we use Connected Papers [101] to check
the relevance and significance of the study. We read through not only peer-reviewed
papers but also official websites and white papers to get the most accurate and up-to-
date information and exclude those without experimental prototypes and testing results.
If two studies shared similar ideas, the first proposal of the creative idea was selected.
Finally, we intend to combine the focused application scenarios of all the selected projects
to cover all the credentialing processes mentioned in Section 3.2.1. The selected use cases
are listed below in chronological order from 2016 to 2021 to examine how blockchain-
based credentialing solutions have evolved.
1. Blockcerts (2016) [102], the world’s first and most widespread blockchain-based
educaiton credentialing platform, was developed jointly by the MIT Media Lab and
Learning Machine, the key function of which is to support credentialing issuance
and verification.
2. EduCTX (2018) [20, 103], the first project to build on the regional regulation
framework – the European Credit Transfer and Accumulation System – creates
tokens as learning credits to facilitate learning credits transfer, accumulation and
verification.
3. E2C-Chain (2019) [22], the first and only project that considered social welfare
maximization, introduced an incentives model to create a peer-to-peer verifica-
tion system of education and employment skills and used ZK-SNARK to protect
learners’ sensitive data.
4. BOLL (2019) [21], Blockchain of Learning Log, fully relies on three types of smart
contracts to track learners’ learning records and support transitions between in-
stitutions.
5. QualiChain (2019) [23, 104], the most representative Pan-European digital edu-
cation credential infrastructure funded by the European Union, covers four appli-
cation scenarios to target four groups of clients: supporting lifelong learning for
30
learners, assisting curriculum design for schools, staffing for the public sector, and
providing HR consultancy for enterprises.
6. Docschain (2020) [24], the first one to integrate Internet of Things (IoT) devices,
supports traditional paper credentials uploading on chain.
7. TolFob (2021) [25], as the first to propose a conceptual learning application model
and the protocol went through intensive testing (98,181 teachers and students, 38
courses, total 40,708 times of learning activity).
This study does not aim to conduct a comprehensive literature review but rather a cross-
project analysis to explore potential barriers that hindered scaled adoption. We devel-
oped a four-layer comparison framework by integrating the design pattern of “blockchain
within a software architecture” [105, 106] with system architectures of selected educa-
tion use cases, aiming to provide guidelines for developing education applications on
blockchains. The framework includes four layers: the prerequisite layer, application
layer, interoperability layer, and blockchain layer (see Figure 3.2).
Figure 3.2: Four-layer Comparison Metrics for EduCredentials Applications
3.4.1 Prerequisite layer
This layer indicates core aspects of knowledge required before starting system design,
such as industry analysis, users’ observation and evaluation and users’ requirements
31
specification. Involving users to participate and collaborate in the design process makes
the system or product more likely to be accepted and adopted by more users [107].
Therefore, this layer of work lays a foundation for developing an effective and highly
user-accepted system or product[107].
However, from our observation (see the first column in Figure 2), this layer of work has
not gained enough attention so far. We specify two weak points as examples. Firstly,
there exists a gap between design assumptions and users’ actual habits. QualiChain is
the best practitioner of prerequisite studies among the studies reviewed here through
conducting numerous workshops to elicit user requirements [104]. Even so, from their
most recent report of completion and reflection, their users reported a certain extent of
difficulties when using the application [104]. It may indicate the requirements elicited
from the lab workshops may still differ from what users actually do in their daily prac-
tices. Secondly, the targeted clients may not be the real beneficiaries. The current
blockchain solutions primarily target HEIs as the main clients for adopting their DApps.
However, it is the students, not HEIs, who bear the most cost of the credentialing (e.g.,
the My eQual platform charge HEI $2-$5 per credential, but learners pay $21 per cre-
dential [12]). For most HEIs, choosing blockchain-based tools is an alternative option
but not a mandatory policy. The institution’s policy can seriously influence the speed
of blockchain adoption when competing with other educational priorities. Such anal-
ysis does not intend to stop us from providing blockchain solutions for HEIs, but to
encourage researchers and developers to pay more attention to evaluate targeted user
groups.
Therefore, systematic user involvement strategies are considered necessary in this layer
to learn about users’ requirements, values and habits within real-life contexts. There
are numerous user involvement studies currently available, but since it is not the focus
topic of our current study, it is not detailed and elaborated further.
3.4.2 Application layer
Users can leverage the benefits of blockchain technology through interacting with the
application layer [106]. This layer focuses on what performances and functions are
formalized within the DApps as solutions to fulfil users’ particular requirements. In
practice, the execution of the functions under blockchain scope is usually supported by
32
smart contracts, which will be discussed in Section IV-D(2), and the functioning cost
will be mentioned in Section IV-D(4).
Compared with the previous layer, this layer flourished with discussions of various func-
tions (see Figure 2). However, a majority of current projects work on their own functional
structure and fall into a solitary development situation. Briefly, Blockcerts supports the
elementary function of credentials issuance and verification. E2C creates a peer-to-peer
endorsement function in the verification process. Both of them do not support accumula-
tion of credits, and education transition like EduCTX and BOLL. Although DocsChain
targets improving Blockcerts’ limitations, it did not build on Blockcerts’ standards but
created its own system [24]. The other two projects, Qualichain and ToIFob, even
cover more robust functionality but lead to a more complex system design and a longer
project development cycle. Besides, the Qualichain community involves only European
universities, and ToIFob only connects universities and EduTech vendors in China.
If these projects could extend on each other’s functions and share their clients’ resources,
there would be less resources wasted, and blockchain adoption could move to the next
level – a collaborative global ecosystem. Therefore, inspired by [106], we suggest future
developers should consider the following designing principles: (i) modularity: the indi-
vidual application can work as a functional unit that can be customized and plugged into
a larger ecosystem; (ii) evolvability: the credentialing system can adapt to the increased
requirements of various stakeholders and ever-changing social environment; (iii) separa-
tion of concerns: an extra layer of freedom that single modular failure or replacement
would not affect the whole system. Creating a sustainable and scalable credentialing
ecosystem is a complex and challenging process that not only requires proactive plan-
ning of functionality and flexibility but also considerations of business elaboration and
organization development.
3.4.3 Interoperability layer
Interoperability has an extensive scope of definitions that have not achieved global in-
teroperability standards yet [108]. In education settings, based on current blockchain
solutions, interoperability can be interpreted as the ability to enhance interoperation
and data exchanges between various education entities, such as education regulations
33
(e.g. curriculum frameworks or credit transfer standards), HEIs information manage-
ment systems (IMS) and blockchain-based education applications. The enhancement
of interoperability can promote: application portability, cooperation between different
DApps [108] and the integration of the whole education ecosystem.
EduCTX is the only one that shows consideration of legality and regulation interop-
erability. It creates tokens that are consistent with the European Credit Transfer and
Accumulation System (ECTS) agreed on by the EU member states [20]. QualiChain
claims to achieve semantic interoperability through ontologies [104]. Most studies use
APIs to interact with HEIs IMS for retrieving learners’ education information. However,
none of the initiatives considers interoperation with other counterparts, which leads to
the solitary development phenomenon where each credentialing system operates solely
on a different blockchain within its isolated community.
Achieving interoperability at all levels is a complex mission with an inadequate amount
of studies at this point and has not yet achieved a global agreement on a standardized
interoperability architecture. But it does not mean we cannot make any effort to im-
prove it when designing an interoperable blockchain system. Practical interoperability
strategies may include processes of standardization of the building blocks, such as data
formats, transmissions and workflows [108]. For example, the latest version of Block-
cert has been upgraded to align with the Verifiable Credentials (VCs) and Decentralized
Identifiers (DIDs) standards – two powerful data models defined by the WWW Con-
sortium (W3C) that can support interoperability [102]. Another feasible strategy could
be to replace the centralized data storage with a cross-blockchain data storage solution,
such as the InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) – a type of distributed file system that
facilitates interoperability between dApps [108]. Therefore, we should leverage these
interoperability-supported tools to create more opportunities for blockchain adoption
and a more cooperative environment between different initiatives.
3.4.4 Blockchain layer
This section compares the selected solutions in blockchain layer based on different as-
pects: types of blockchain, smart contracts, data storage and economic cost.
Types of Blockchain
34
Most of the current application models are built on public platforms such as Bitcoin
and Ethereum, where anyone can join without entry requirements. This mechanism
can indeed encourage more participants, but also bring along with serious issues. For
example, the original prototype of Blockcert was built on Bitcoin, which has been proved
that a fake issuer can pass all the verification steps as long as holding a valid key
pair [17]. Therefore, after 2020, blockchain practitioners of education industry tend
to choose permissioned blockchain, where accessibility limits and some authorization
mechanism exist to give different roles to different authorized identities. Docschain
adopted a mixed-level of ownership, where the system’s control right is assigned to
semi-decentralized consortium members, and membership selection right belongs to a
trusted central entity [24]. In addition, public blockchains typically use consensus based
on “proof of work” and cryptocurrency incentives, the mining process of which has
been challenged as wasting of resource and energy. So many environmentally friendlier
alternatives have been created, such as Proof-of-Stake (PoS), Proof-of-Authority (PoA)
and Proof-of-Capacity (PoC). EduCTX adopted DPoS (a type of PoS consensus), where
no computing power is required by the participated node [20].
Smart Contract
The earliest credentialing application built on Bitcoin can only support basic functions
of credentialing issuance and verification. As more complex functionality structure is
required, adoptions move to smart-contract supported platforms include Ethereum Vir-
tual Machine and Hyperledger Fabric’s Chaincode. Thanks to the introduction of Smart
contracts, applied functionalities of blockchains have been largely extended [95]. In fact,
the project BOLL uses three types of smart contracts, namely, registrar learning provider
contract (RLPC), learner-learning provider contract (LLPC), and index contract (IC),
to realize the full function of learning data transition between different institutions
and solve the cold-start problem in learning analytics systems [21]. Furthermore, Hy-
perledger Fabric involves the blockchain specific programming language Solidity into
chaincode, which enables a more user-friendly and commonly-seen programming lan-
guage [109]. This innovation brings more technical feasibility to general IT staff from
institutions who may not be equipped with skills in the blockchain language.
Data Storage The selected educational applications either choose to store hashes of
credential information on-chain or choose a third party database, such as MangoDB, for
35
data storage. So instead of storing education data on-chain, the BOLL project choose to
use MongoDB, a central database, to store learning data in order to improve performance
and frequent data accessibility [21].
Economic feasibility In addition to the technical issues, blockchain-related economic
issues can also affect the feasibility of implementation. The economic feasibility includes
considerations of three aspects: the cost of running blockchain, the built-in economic
efficiency model, and the cost of adapting into the blockchain infrastructure. Firstly,
transaction costs have been proven to be higher for public blockchains than the private
ones [106]. The test results of BOLL indicate every learning record updated on chain
can cause certain amount of fluctuated transaction fee measured by gases. So we need
to take transaction cost into account when designing the application. Secondly, from
a blockchain for social good perspective, we can embed an economic efficiency model
into the prototype design to minimize social cost within the system. E2C-Chain has
set a great example of this by adopting Nash equilibrium for selection of verifiers and
price setting [22]. The last cost consideration is social resources that can be invested
in establishing blockchain infrastructure. On the one hand, whether there is enough
funding and human resources may effect the success of establishment. On the other
hand, it is difficult to measure and predict the cost of a new technology adoption on an
industry-level.
Blockchains deployed in practice have to match with one’s particular business mode.
Every decision and action along the adoption procedure, people have to face a number
of feasibility considerations. In practical scenario, considerations are not only including
the above-mentioned aspects: types of blockchain, smart contracts and on-chain or
off-chain data storage, but also regarding of incentives mechanism, privacy protection,
signature authorization, and asynchronous network effect etc.
3.5 Chapter Summary
This chapter examined the potential of blockchain technology to the identified challenges,
aligning with RQ1. To assess the applicability of blockchain in this domain, a four-layer
evaluation framework was proposed and applied to selected blockchain-based educa-
tion projects. The comparative analysis revealed both opportunities and limitations of
36
current implementations, contributing insights into factors hindering the adoption and
scalability of these solutions that directly addresses RQ2. The findings of this chapter
are intended to raise awareness among blockchain practitioners and researchers about
the existing gaps and provide guidance for the design and development of more effective
blockchain solutions in education. However, this study acknowledges its limitations. It
focuses on a small sample of selected cases, which restricts its ability to generalize find-
ings to the broader blockchain development landscape. Furthermore, this study does
not propose a specific new solution, as its primary aim is to serve as a foundational
exploration for subsequent research.
Some results of this chapter have been published in the 2022 IEEE International Con-
ference on Blockchain [29]. This chapter lays the groundwork for Chapter 4, which
transitions from analysis to practical development. The next chapter addresses the
socio-technical barriers to blockchain adoption ( RQ3) and presents a tailored engineer-
ing methodology to develop scalable and user-friendly blockchain credentialing systems
(RQ4).
Chapter 4
CValid: An Educational
Credentialing System Designed
via BOSE-HAP
“The search for new techniques must be regarded as carried out by the human
community as a whole.” — Alan Turing
This chapter presents the research outcomes of Phase Two, addressing RQ3 andRQ4.
It introduces the Blockchain-Oriented Software Engineering Approach for Higher Adop-
tion Possibility (BOSE-HAP) , a novel framework designed to bridge the gap between
blockchain’s technical potential and its practical application. Through the application of
BOSE-HAP , we co-designed CValid , a blockchain-based credentialing system, with key
stakeholders from industries and institutions. Through this collaborative and usability-
driven approach, the chapter demonstrates how stakeholder engagement at every stage
of design and development can enhance blockchain adoption in the education sector.
4.1 Introduction
While blockchain technology has shown significant promise across various domains, its
adoption in real-world applications faces substantial challenges. As discussed in Chapter
1, these challenges include but are not limited to technical barriers, human factors, and
37
38
socio-contextual limitations. Besides, existing blockchain software engineering frame-
works lack practical insights, hindering widespread adoption and scalability. To address
these challenges , we introduce a Blockchain-oriented Software Engineering Approach for
Higher Adoption Possibility (BOSE-HAP) in this chapter. BOSE-HAP emphasizes col-
laboration, reflective thinking, and iterative development, aiming to bolster implementa-
tion consistency and stimulate industry adoption. We have applied this approach in the
design, development, and launch of a blockchain credentialing product, CValid.org , in
the context of a university-level summer school. The product achieves industry-accepted
System Usability Scores and has seen successful real-world deployment. In addition, this
study embedded usability considerations throughout the process, involved a total of 112
stakeholders across different development stages, with 25 of them participating in our
in-depth interviews and usability testing. Drawing from our firsthand experience and
industrial-grounded findings, we deliver 8reflections and propose 5best practice sugges-
tions relevant to blockchain adoption. We believe these insights will provide invaluable
guidance for both academic researchers and industry practitioners involved in the field
of blockchain technology.
Our study aims to enhance blockchain application adoption in industries and addresses
the identified gaps in three ways: 1) incorporating usability considerations consistently
in the research and development stages; 2) devising a systematic engineering approach to
steer our project’s development, validating this framework through multiple iterations;
and 3) deriving implementation guidelines from our firsthand experiences of collabora-
tion with industry stakeholders and blockchain developers. This work presents the first
end-to-end implementation documented in the literature for constructing blockchain-
based applications that explore adoption barriers, delivering tangible user value during
the credentialing process. The study offers several contributions to both practice and
research, as follows:
4.1.1 Contributions
•We propose a Blockchain-oriented Software Engineering Approach for Higher Adop-
tion Possibility (BOSE-HAP) . It fills the shortage of tailored situational engineer-
ing approaches by integrating design-based research and social-technical grounded
39
theory with a portfolio of DApps engineering approaches. The fundamental prin-
ciples of this method — collaboration, reflective thinking, and repeated iteration
— facilitate technical implementation along with socio-technical considerations,
which are essential for successful deployment and widespread adoption of DApps
in the industry.
•We design, develop and launch a blockchain credentialing product (named CValid.org )
to support a university-level summer school’s credentialing activities. A total of

4.2 Blockchain-oriented Software Engineering Approach for
Higher Adoption Possibility (BOSE-HAP)
To guide this holistic study and develop the project in a systematic way, we propose
a tailored framework: Blockchain-oriented Software Engineering Approach for Higher
Adoption Possibility (BOSE-HAP) (illustrated in Figure 4.1). As an overview, BOSE-
HAP consists of three core layers: the design-based thinking flow (the blue layer), the
40
engineering workflow (the green layer), and the iteration stages (the orange layer). The
design-based thinking layer acts as a philosophical guide for our specialized engineer-
ing procedures, drawing inspiration from the principles of design-based research. The
engineering workflow layer outlines specific engineering steps, which also inform the
structure of the subsequent sections of this paper. The iterative layer, comprised of
analysis iteration, engineering iteration and reflective iteration, highlights the dynamic
and interconnected nature of each step, suggesting that actions should not operate in
isolation but may loop back and enhance the system based on reflections from each
stage. The BOSE-HAP is established on a range of methods, which can be grouped into
three categories:
1.Research theoretical underpinnings: we adopt a design-based research method
(DBR) [110–113] and social-technical grounded theory (STGT) [114, 115] to build
the theoretical foundation of our study. They were selected for their specific
attributes and advantages in probing the intricate socio-technical dynamics of
blockchain applications within an educational context.
2.Blockchain application engineering approaches : We select some key ele-
ments from some existing blockchain-oriented software engineering approaches,
known as BOSE or BSS [39, 40, 116], for the development of the system.
3.Testing methods: System Usability Scales (SUS) [117] and Think Aloud [118]
are employed for the assessment of the system’s efficacy and user-friendliness.
The rest of this section introduces the three categories of theories we adopted and
explains the rationale behind their selection.
4.2.1 Research Theoretical Underpinnings
Our study is grounded in two research methodologies: DBR and STGT. DBR has been
used widely in the fields of instructional design and human-computer interaction, and
it exhibits the following characteristics [110–113]: 1) the emphasis on iterative cycles of
analysis, design, and implementation; 2) designs are conducted in real-world settings;
and 3) the process typically begins with expert consultations, examination of examples,
and case studies of current practices. On the other hand, STGT is particularly effective
41

Possibility (BOSE-HAP)
for exploring complex socio-technical phenomena in software engineering [114, 115]. The
basic STGT stage involves open coding, constant comparison, and basic memoing. The
constant comparison applies an inductive approach, escalating codes to concepts, and
subsequently to (sub-)category levels (we exemplify how to achieve this in Figure 4.8 un-
der Section 4.5.3). In our proposed BOSE-HAP framework, we use DBR to orchestrate
the design-based thinking flow. Concurrently, we use STGT basic stage techniques to
ground industry-specific data, facilitate data analysis, and generate reflective concepts.
Both DBR and STGT share a common philosophical underpinning of iterative develop-
ment, encapsulating the cyclic nature of real-world problem-solving scenarios. As such,
combining both methods empowers us to continuously adapt and refine the blockchain
application, responding aptly to emerging insights and evolving user needs.
4.2.2 Blockchain Application Engineering Approaches
A software design framework can support reflective inquiry in design-based research
[112]. The use of a well-designed systematic engineering approach for blockchain systems
(commonly known as ‘BOSE’ or ‘BBS’ for short) can improve efficiency, better meet user
satisfaction and reduce unforeseen security and other errors [39, 40, 116]. As our goal
is to build a system that can serve a global community, a systematic design approach
can help researchers and developers to document clear development pathways and lead
to more efficient iterations in each development stage. A recent study by [39] provides a
42
comprehensive review of BOSE frameworks and offers a detailed account of the critical
tasks involved within the BOSE procedure. We selected certain elements from the
existing BOSE models [39, 40, 116], integrating reflective inquiry and user involvement
at various engineering stages, to propose the BOSE-HAP. This engineering procedure
serves as the backbone of this paper (as depicted in the green layer of Figure 4.1) and
is elaborated upon from Section 4.3 onward.
4.2.3 Usability Testing Methods
To drive an iterative design process, we employ two established usability testing methods:
SUS and the Think-Aloud technique. SUS is a recognized and standardized method to
assess usability factors such as efficiency, behavioural intentions, and satisfaction using
the Likert scale questionnaire [117]. Validation of the SUS has been performed with
a sample size of 20 participants, making it a “fairly quick” approach [119]. On the
other hand, Think-Aloud provides insight into users’ mental processes, which can be
valuable in identifying specific usability issues. This method has been demonstrated as
an effective way to gather task-related data in an unbiased manner [118], as participants
would be verbalizing their thoughts and actions as they completed the tasks. We collect
SUS scores both after a quick test and during an in-depth Think Aloud interview. Thus,
the usability scores are collected throughout the user testing stage. As for the Think
Aloud, We design a list of credentialing tasks for the participants to complete, which
simulated the entire process of issuing and obtaining credentials. Then, we use STGT
to analyse the data gathered from the interview transcripts generated from think-aloud
process. Both quantitative and qualitative analyses of the SUS and Think Aloud are
presented in Section 4.5.

4.3.1 Industry Investigation
We examine the credentialing landscape from two levels: a theoretical level and an
industry-based inquiry. Theoretically, the credentialing landscape encompasses four dis-
tinct stakeholders: education providers act as issuers by defining and issuing credentials;
learners are the primary entities who attain, manage, and utilize these credentials; cer-
tifying authorities serve as witnesses to affirm the authenticity of these credentials; and
recruiters act as verifiers who verify the authenticity of the credentials as an assessment
of applicants’ relevant skills (as detailed in Chapter 3 Section 3.2).
For the industry-based inquiry, we focus exclusively on recruiters for two reasons: First,
recruiters play a pivotal role in verifying the authenticity of credentials and directly
influence the hiring process. Their responsibilities require them to assess the trustwor-
thiness and relevance of credentials, making them primary stakeholders in credential
verification systems. Second, unlike learners, recruiters often encounter systemic inef-
ficiencies, such as time-consuming verification processes and limited tools for detecting
fraudulent credentials, which makes them ideal participants for exploring pain points
and identifying areas for improvement.
Participants and Methods
The industry-based inquiry aims to validate the credentialing pain points within the
real-world context. We conduct semi-structured interviews with 12 senior recruiters
from 10 different industries with an average of 6-10 years of experience. Their working
background can cover nine industries: headhunters, tertiary institutions, digital media,
investment consulting, oil and mining, consumer goods, non-for-profits, and real estate
and information technology (participants’ demographics see Appendix Table A.1) . Our
designed interview questions relate to areas such as 1) recruitment procedure, 2) verifica-
tion criteria and 3) working challenges in their daily practice (interview guide accessible
at: Recruiters interview).

4.3.2 User Value Evaluation
Since learners are the primary users of credentials, this user evaluation focuses on un-
derstanding learners’ needs and perceptions of credentials. Products with “superior
customer value” and a “well-defined” product concept have a greater likelihood of adop-
tion success [120]. To ensure that our blockchain solution can provide genuine value to
learners, we conduct the following work: define the customer value metrics and evalua-
tion measures, collect survey data, and present the evaluation results.
Customer Value Metrics
Based on a widely-adopted framework for creating customer value [120], we define cus-
tomer value as being derived from satisfying three fundamental needs: functional needs,
emotional needs, and cost needs. In other words, our product or service can create pos-
itive customer value by successfully fulfilling these basic needs. We elaborate on each
need’s definitions as follows.
•Functional needs - functional needs refer to the practical requirements that con-
sumers seek to fulfil when searching for products or services. This perceived value
positively influences the consumer’s willingness to pay for the product or service.
To measure “functional needs”, we collect participants’ agreement on two state-
ments: 1) “Credentials are important and helpful for my study and career” and 2)
“I am willing to invest time and money in credentials”.
•Emotional needs - these needs arise from a product’s ability to evoke or sustain
feelings, such as comfort, security, excitement, romance, passion, fear, or guilt. We
measure this demand by collecting users’ positive and negative feelings about their
46
interactions with credentials, such as “I believe it’s crucial to keep my credentials
safe”, “I am concerned about losing or damaging credentials” and “I worry about
privacy leakage”.
•Economic needs, or cost value, refer to the product’s ability to decrease customers’
economic or psychological costs associated with a task or to assist them in making
faster and less stressful decisions. This area of needs is defined as being closely tied
to people’s pain points, reflecting a more immediate demand for an innovative new
tool. The measured statements include: “I believe recovering damaged credentials
is a complex process” and “I believe certifying my credentials is a complex process”.
To measure the three metrics, we use a 5-point Likert scale to collect participants’
agreement on each of the statements. All statements within one metric are assumed to
carry equal weight. We establish a threshold of 3 as the minimum average mean for
each metric. If the average mean for the set of statements exceeded 3, and the collected
data demonstrated a normal distribution, we reject the null hypothesis, and accept the
alternative hypothesis that there exists a verifiable demand for innovative credentialing
tools.
